new_statements.quote: Stress generally falls on the first syllable of the word. Prefixes are usually not stressed and stress then falls on the second syllable. This also applies to words where the prefix is no longer productive. A few other examples do not conform to the usual stress pattern but this has no semantic significance. As stress is not fully predictable it is marked in this chapter on all words where stress is not on the first syllable. Stress on the first syllable, which is the main type, is seen in: /a/ ['a.nu] 'man' /etok/ ['ɛ.tɔk] 'talk' /βogo/ ['βɔ.gɔ] 'pig' /tiptip/ ['tɪp.tɪp] 'heavy'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's initial-stress (StressTyp2, initial stress) placement and refines it: the initial pattern is the 'main type', prefixes are extrametrical so prefixed words surface with second-syllable stress, and a residue of lexical exceptions makes stress 'not fully predictable' though non-contrastive. This is almost certainly the source behind the StressTyp2 record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the word as the main pattern. Prefixes are normally unstressed, so prefixed words (including those whose prefix is no longer productive) carry stress on the second syllable, e.g. /na'ri/ 'they', /su'guk/ 'to me', /pa'loŋani/ 'hear it'. A few unprefixed words are also second-syllable stressed (/ma'sut/ 'bush', /i'naŋ/ 'go', /pa'pais/ 'quickly'); these do not conform to the usual pattern and stress is described as 'not fully predictable' but carries no semantic (contrastive) significance.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only a single primary stress is transcribed per word.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Prefixed words, including fossilised prefixes, are stressed on the second syllable (prefix unstressed). (2) 'A few other examples' with second-syllable stress that do not conform to the usual pattern (/ma'sut/ 'bush', /i'naŋ/ 'go', /pa'pais/ 'quickly'); author marks stress on all non-initially stressed words because stress is 'not fully predictable'. Section 2.2.2 Intonation (p. 30) adds two contrastive sentence intonations (statement/command: final syllable lower tone; question: final syllable higher tone), which is phrase-level, not word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Beaumont 1974 describes the Tigak of New Ireland (Kavieng area) as a whole; no dialect is singled out in the stress section. The SIL listing targets ISO tgc = Tigak, same identity.

new_statements.relation_note: The OPD's stress paragraph is word-for-word the catalog quote (Beaumont's wording; the OPD bibliography cites Beaumont 1969-1979 and his SIL Ukarumpa manuscripts), so it AGREES with the fixed: initial syllable record and the Beaumont 1974/1979 statements held by the project, adding only that unstressed /e/ centralises. Jenkins 1998 REFINES for the Island dialect: default initial stress but weight-sensitive ('first or heavy': a long vowel/diphthong in the second syllable takes the stress, codas weightless), root-initial stress under prefixation with a two-syllable initial window (WISC), compounds strictly initial. This weight condition is not in the catalog's fixed-strict coding; whether it…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Central dialect (OPD, wording identical to Beaumont): primary stress on the first syllable of the word; prefixes (including fossilised ones) are unstressed so prefixed words carry stress on the second syllable (= root-initial); a few lexical exceptions, never contrastive in meaning; /e/ is centralised in unstressed syllables. Island dialect (Jenkins 1998): 'first or heavy' stress: stress the first syllable unless the second syllable has a complex nucleus (long vowel or diphthong), which then takes the stress ('tapak 'lightning' vs ta'paak 'leprosy'); coda consonants carry no weight; within a complex nucleus stress sits on the first vowel; Root Stress Rule: under prefixation and reduplication stress stays on the root's stressed syllable (;'ka.mus, ma.'tug) unless that would put it on the third or later syllable of the word, in which case it goes to the word-initial syllable (Word Initial Stress Constraint: 'lat.mat.tug, ';ku.ruul, 'sak.sa.kai), modelled as cyclic assignment; suffixes never affect stress; summary: 'Stress is primarily on the first heavy syllable of a word, with the constraint against (primary) stress occurring more than two syllables from the beginning of the word.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: OPD: nothing. Jenkins 1998 (p.26): 'I have not speculated on the occurrence of secondary stress' for lack of data; serial verbs also not analysed.
new_statements.exceptions: OPD: unstressed prefixes (also non-productive ones) give second-syllable stress; 'a few other examples do not conform.. no semantic significance'. Jenkins: heavy (complex-nucleus) second syllable attracts stress; two non-productive prefixes ve- 'related pair' and ta- 'stative' are stressed ('vet.ti.vu, 'tat.sa.vat) because reanalysed as part of the root; Compound Stress Rule: compounds always initial-stressed even before a heavy syllable ('pat.liu 'walk past' vs intensifier pa.'liu 'very much'); long syllables beyond the two-syllable window are unstressed (';ku.ruul).
new_statements.identity_note: OPD: Tigak, Central dialect (Omo, Kavieng, New Hanover), Kavieng, New Ireland Province, the variety Beaumont described. Jenkins 1998: Island Tigak (the island dialect), her own analysis from SIL fieldwork. Both are Tigak [tgc], tiga1245.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction of the catalog. The SIL OPD (Central dialect) repeats Beaumont's statement verbatim: stress on the first syllable, prefixes unstressed (then second syllable), a few non-contrastive exceptions = the fixed: initial syllable record. Jenkins 1998, describing the Island dialect, keeps initial stress as the default but makes it weight-sensitive: a complex nucleus (long vowel or diphthong, codas weightless) in the second syllable attracts the stress ('tapak 'lightning' vs ta'paak 'leprosy'), prefixed words keep root-initial stress unless that would fall beyond the second syllable of the word (then word-initial), and compounds are always initial-stressed. That is a refinement the catalog's 'fixed-strict' coding does not capture (a quantity-sensitive first-or-second-syllable window for Island Tigak); it may also be what Beaumont's 'a few other examples do not conform' refers to, but neither source says so.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is present verbatim (modulo scanned letter-spacing) in the PL-B58 scan we hold at the stated place: section 2.2.1 Stress, printed p. 18 = PDF page 30. (2) The source is the language's only reference grammar (Beaumont 1979, PL B-58, xi+163 pp, phonology chapter), i.e. the top item of Glottolog's descriptive bibliography; the only longer work is the same author's 1974 ANU thesis, which I downloaded (open access) and which carries the identical stress paragraph on p. 29. Beaumont 1988 (downloaded) is silent; Beaumont 1989 is a verb-phrase syntax article. No later phonological or instrumental study of Tigak was found in Glottolog, the ANU repository, or Lynch-Ross-Crowley 2002; (3) Coding: initi
